Be gracious, Soul of all dharma, perishable and imperishable, Maheshvara, spoken of through conceptions such as Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
brahmapuran:192:52	Of indescribable nature, of indescribable purpose, of indescribable name, I bow to you, Supreme Lord.
brahmapuran:192:53	Where, lord, no conceptions of name, birth and the like exist, that is Supreme Brahman, eternal, unchanging; you are unborn.
brahmapuran:192:54	Since without conception there is no grasping of any object, therefore you are praised by names such as Krishna, Achyuta, Ananta, Vishnu.
brahmapuran:192:55	Soul of all, unborn, you are the gods through these differentiations; you are the whole world, you alone are the universe; Soul of the universe, free of all differences of change, there is nothing else apart from you in everything.
brahmapuran:192:56	You are Brahma, Pashupati, Aryaman, Vidhatri, Dhatri, lord of the thirty, wind and fire, lord of waters, lord of wealth and Death; one, with a divided self, you protect the world by differences of power.
brahmapuran:192:57	You, as the Sun, create and destroy the universe, and this expanse is made of your qualities, unborn; the supreme form called 'being', the imperishable — to that knowledge-self, existent and non-existent, I bow.
brahmapuran:192:58	Om, salutation to Vasudeva, and salutation to Sankarshana; salutation to you, Pradyumna; salutation to you, Aniruddha.
Having thus praised Krishna in the water, that Yadava worshipped the Lord of all with mental incense and flowers.
Abandoning other objects and fixing his mind there, he stayed long as Brahman, then ceased from the samadhi.
Considering himself as one whose task is done, best of Brahmins, he came out of the Yamuna's water to the chariot again.
He saw Rama and Krishna standing as before; Krishna said to Akrura, whose eyes were amazed:
What wonder was seen by you, Akrura, in the Yamuna's water, since your eyes are seen to be wide with amazement?

The wonder, Achyuta, that I saw there in the water, I see here too, standing embodied before me.
brahmapuran:192:65	The world is of wondrous form, of whose great-souled one it is; being with you, Krishna, who are devoted to wonders, I have met him.
brahmapuran:192:66	So what of this? Let us go to Mathura, Madhusudana. I fear Kamsa; shame on the birth of one who lives on another's food.
Having said so, he urged the horses swift as wind and arrived in the evening at Mathura city. Seeing Mathura, that Yadava said to Krishna and Rama:
You two mighty ones go on foot; I alone enter by chariot. You two must go to Vasudeva's house; for your sake the old man is cast off by Kamsa.
Having said so Akrura entered Mathura city; Rama and Krishna entered and came to the royal road.
Looked at by women and men with delighted eyes, the two heroes went at ease, like young elephants arrived.
Seeing a washerman wandering, a dyer, they two asked for lovely garments of their kind.
That washerman of Kamsa, risen by his master's favour and astonished, spoke many words of insult loudly to Rama and Keshava.
Then Krishna with a blow of his palm in anger struck the head of that wicked washerman to the ground.
Having killed him and taken the clothes, Krishna and Rama in yellow and blue garments, glad, went to the garland-maker's house.
The garland-maker, his eyes wide, much amazed, thought, "Whose are these two, and whence have they come?"
Seeing the two wearing yellow and blue garments, most charming, he then supposed that two gods had come to earth.
Asked for flowers by the two with blooming lotus faces, he bowed his head to the ground, supporting himself with his hands.
The two lords, gracious-faced, have come to my house; I am blessed; I shall worship them, said that garland-maker to them.
Then, with glad face, he gave them flowers as they wished, these lovely ones, enticing them.
Bowing again and again, that best of garland-makers gave the two lovely, fragrant, pure flowers.
Krishna, pleased, gave the garland-maker a boon: "Good one, Shri, resting on me, will never leave you.
Gentle one, there will be no loss of strength or loss of wealth for you, and your lineage of sons and grandsons will last as long as earth and sun.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures, at the end, by my grace, you will obtain remembrance of me and reach a divine world.
Your mind will be on dharma at all times, good one, and those born in your lineage will have long life.
The birth of your offspring will not meet faults such as calamity, fortunate one, as long as the sun exists."
Having said so, Krishna with Baladeva left his house, best of sages, honoured by the garland-maker.
A great cry arose in all the arenas thereafter, from the world's amazement: "This is Krishna, this is Balabhadra."

This is he by whom the terrible night-roaming Putana was slain, by whom the cart was thrown and the twin arjunas broken.
brahmapuran:193:34	This is he who as a boy danced mounted on the Naga Kaliya; by whom Mount Govardhana was held for seven nights.
brahmapuran:193:35	This is Achyuta, by whom the evil Arishta, Dhenuka and Keshi were slain by the great-souled one in sport.

And this is his mighty-armed elder brother Baladeva, who goes in front at ease, delighting the minds and eyes of women.
brahmapuran:193:37	He is the one whom the wise who see the meaning of the Puranas say will lift out the Yadava line that has sunk, the cowherd.
brahmapuran:193:38	He is a portion of Vishnu, the source of all births, descended on earth, surely the remover of the earth's burden.
While Rama and Krishna were thus described by the citizens, at that moment Devaki's breasts, wet with the milk of affection, were pained.
Looking at her two sons as at a great festival, Vasudeva became young, old age having left him.
The women of the king's inner apartments, with eyes wide, and the crowd of city women did not tire of gazing at them.

Friends, see Krishna's lotus-eyed face too, adorned with drops of sweat-water from the effort of the elephant fight,
brahmapuran:193:43	like a blooming lotus sprinkled with dew; make your eyes' birth fruitful, putting aside the imperishable.
brahmapuran:193:44	See this chest of the boy, marked with Shrivatsa, the abode of the world, and the pair of arms, destroyers of the enemy, fair one.
brahmapuran:193:45	Balabhadra, as Mushtika and Chanura and others leap, is a sight for slight laughter.
brahmapuran:193:46	Friends, see: this Hari comes for a duel with Chanura; are there not elders here who do what is fitting?
brahmapuran:193:47	Where is Hari, delicate-bodied, turning toward youth, and where this great Asura, with a body firm as adamant?
brahmapuran:193:48	These two newly youthful, very charming ones are in the arena, and the Daitya wrestlers led by Chanura are very terrible.
brahmapuran:193:49	This is a great breach by the judges of the duel, that a fight between a boy and strongmen is ignored by the arbiters.
While the city women spoke thus, the Lord Hari, shaking the earth, rained a flood of joy on the people.
When Balabhadra, slapping his arm, leaped gracefully, the earth was not cracked at each step; that was wonderful.
Then Krishna of immeasurable valour fought with Chanura, and Baladeva with the Daitya Mushtika, skilled in wrestling.
With blows of collision, throws, fists, and strikes like thunderbolts of wedges, Hari fought with Chanura,
and with those arising from feet and rubbings; a great battle took place between the two, weaponless and very terrible and fierce,
to be accomplished by their own strength and life, in the presence of the festival of the assembly. As Chanura fought with Hari,
so much the more he suffered loss of life at the front, and not of kin; Krishna too fought with him in sport, he who consists of the world.
Seeing the loss of strength and the increase in Chanura and Krishna, Kamsa, in anger and distress, moving his hand on his own remaining hand,
intent on rage, had the instruments stopped. When the mridangas and other instruments were forbidden at that moment,
divine instruments in the sky sounded many times: "Victory, Govinda! Kill the Danava Chanura, Keshava!"
Thus the gods, hidden, delighted, praised. Having played a long time with Chanura, Madhusudana,
lifting him up, whirled him for his killing, with effort; having whirled the Daitya wrestler a hundred times, the conqueror of foes
dashed him on the ground, his life gone in the sky; dashed on the ground by him, Chanura broke into a hundred pieces
and made the earth a great mire of flowing blood. Baladeva, mighty, then fought with Mushtika, as Hari with Chanura,
and he striking him on the head with his fist and on the chest with his knee,
felled him to the ground and crushed him, his life gone. Krishna again felled the mighty wrestler-king Toshalaka
to the earth with a blow of his left fist. When Chanura the wrestler was killed and Mushtika felled,
and Toshalaka brought to destruction, all the wrestlers fled. Then both Krishna and Sankarshana leaped in the arena,
delighted, forcibly dragging the cowherds of their own age. Kamsa too, his eyes red with anger, said loudly to the tall men:

Let these two cowherds be driven out by force from the assembly; let Nanda be seized, the sinner, and quickly bound with chains.
brahmapuran:193:70	Let Vasudeva too be killed with a staff unfit even for an old man; and let the cowherds who leap with Krishna together be struck,
brahmapuran:193:71	and let their cows be taken, and whatever wealth they have. As he thus commanded, Madhusudana, laughing,
leapt up, climbed his platform and swiftly seized Kamsa by the hair, dragged him down, his crown slipping, to the ground.
He felled Kamsa and fell on him, heavy as the support of the entire world, falling upon him.
The king, son of Ugrasena, was made by Krishna to give up his life. Then Madhusudana, seizing the dead one by the hair,
the mighty one dragged Kamsa's body into the middle of the arena; as it was dragged by its great weight, the fall
made by Kamsa's body, swiftly by the great-souled one, a furrow. When Kamsa was seized by Krishna, his brother came angrily;
Sunama was felled in sport by Balabhadra. Then a great cry of alarm arose in all that circle of the arena.
Seeing the lord of Mathura slain in contempt by Krishna, Krishna quickly took hold of the feet of Vasudeva
and of Devaki. The mighty-armed one, with Baladeva as helper, raised them; Vasudeva and Devaki stood bowed to Janardana, remembering the words about his birth:

Be gracious, lord of gods, best of gods, lord; as you have lifted us up by your grace, Keshava,
brahmapuran:193:81	the revered one, worshipped, has descended in my house for the killing of the wicked; by that our family is purified.
brahmapuran:193:82	You are within all beings and abide in all beings; and you exist as the Self of all; from you come past and future.
brahmapuran:193:83	You are worshipped in sacrifice, inconceivable, Achyuta, consisting of all gods; you alone are the sacrifice and the sacrificer, Supreme Lord of sacrifices.
brahmapuran:193:84	That this my mind in you is full of concealment, and Devaki's, in love for a son, is a great mockery.
brahmapuran:193:85	You are the maker of all beings, without beginning or end; and where will this tongue of mine, a mortal, say 'son'?
brahmapuran:193:86	Lord of the world, how, without maya, could he from whom this whole world was born be born of us?
brahmapuran:193:87	In whom all the moving and unmoving world is established — how can he who sleeps in the belly's lap be born from a man?
brahmapuran:193:88	Be gracious, Supreme Lord, protect the universe. By making partial incarnations you are not my son. Lord, the whole world from Brahma to a tree — why do you bewilder it in the mind, Supreme Lord, Self?
brahmapuran:193:89	With sight deluded by maya, thinking 'my son,' out of great fear of Kamsa I carried you to Gokula, I, agitated by fear of the enemy; you grew for me and for the cows, lord of cows.
brahmapuran:193:90	The deeds not to be seen, which are to be done by Rudra, the Maruts, the Ashvins and Shatakratu, you, Vishnu, lord of worlds, have come to us for the benefit of the worlds; supreme delusion has overtaken us.
In all the battles he was defeated by the Yadus; Jarasandha, though stronger, withdrew with small forces.
That the Yadava force was protected many times is the greatness of the presence of a part of Vishnu, the discus-bearer.
It is the sport of the Lord of the world, who has human nature and conduct, that he releases many forms of weapons on enemies.
How great a spread of effort is needed for him who by mind alone makes the creation and dissolution of the world, in destroying his enemy's side?
Yet following the dharma of humans, making peace with the strong, he fights with the weak.
Showing conciliation, giving of gifts, division, and sometimes the stroke of punishment and sometimes flight,
thus he follows the conduct of embodied humans; the sport of the Lord of the world proceeds at his will.
He set out day after day by uninterrupted stages against the Yadavas, angry, to Mathura city, sages.
Krishna also thought: "The Yadava force has been depleted; seeing it, the Magadha will come with the Yavana.
The Magadha's force is weakened; the mighty Kalayavana will kill; so this double calamity for the Yadavas has come.
Therefore I shall build a fortress very hard for the Yadavas to be conquered, where even women could fight, what then Vrishni Yadavas?
Let the wicked enemies not harm the Yadavas further when I am intoxicated or careless, asleep or away."
Having thus reflected, Govinda begged twelve yojanas of the great ocean and built there the city of Dvaraka,
with great gardens, great walls, adorned with hundreds of lakes, crowded with hundreds of ramparts, like Indra's Amaravati.
Bringing the people dwelling in Mathura there, Janardana himself went to Mathura when Kalayavana was near.
With the army encamped outside Mathura, Govinda came out unarmed, and the Yavana saw him.
Knowing him as Vasudeva, the king, with arms as weapons, followed him whom the minds of great yogis cannot reach.
Followed by him Krishna too entered a great cave where the very mighty king Mucukunda lay.
The Yavana also entered, and seeing a man lying on the bed, the evil-minded one struck him with his foot, thinking him Krishna.
As soon as seen by him, the Yavana blazed with fire, sages, born of his anger, and was reduced to ashes at that moment.
For he, having gone in the war of gods and Asuras and conquered the great Asuras, tormented by sleep, asked the gods for a long sleep as a boon.
The gods said: "Whoever wakes you asleep will at once be reduced to ashes by fire from your body."
Having thus burned that sinner, seeing Madhusudana, he said, "Who are you?" He said, "I was born in the lunar race,
son of Vasudeva, born in the Yadu family." Hearing that, Mucukunda too, remembering the words of the old Gargya,
remembered and bowed to him, Hari, Lord of all, and said: "You are known, a portion of Vishnu; you are the Supreme Lord.
Formerly it was told by Gargya that in the twenty-eighth yuga, at the end of Dvapara, Hari's birth would occur in the Yadu line.
You have come, no doubt, as benefactor of mortals; I am not able to bear your great brilliance.
Thus then in a voice deeper than the great ocean's roar he said to him, pleasantly comforted by your feet:
In the great war of gods and Asuras the Daityas, great warriors, could not bear that great brilliance; I too cannot bear that brilliance.
For a creature fallen in worldly existence you are the one supreme refuge; be gracious, remover of the distress of the surrendered; remove my inauspiciousness.
You are the oceans, mountains, rivers and forests, earth, sky, wind, water, fire, and the Purusha.
Higher than the Purusha is all, pervading, with birth as if by conception, devoid of sound and the rest, ageless, free of growth and decay.
From you come immortals, ancestors, Yakshas, Gandharvas and Rakshasas, Siddhas and Apsarases; from you humans, animals and birds,
reptiles and deer, all, and trees; whatever has been or will be here in the moving and unmoving,
formed or formless, gross or subtler, all that you are, maker of the world; nothing exists without you.
Wandering always in this wheel of worldly existence, lord, overcome by the threefold affliction, I have nowhere obtained peace.
Sorrows only, as pleasures, like a pool of mirage-water, were taken up by me, lord, and they became torment for me.
Kingdom, land, army, treasury, allies, children, wives, servants, and the sense-objects beginning with sound, lord —
all this was taken by me with the idea of happiness, imperishable one; in the result it became torment for me, lord of gods.
I attained the course of the world of gods, lord; even the host of gods desired my help; where is eternal peace?
Without worshipping you, the source and abode of all the worlds, by whom, Supreme Lord, is eternal peace attained?
Those whose minds are deluded by your maya, obtaining birth, death, old age and other sins, see in the interval the king of the dead.
Then, bound by hundreds of nooses in the hells, they obtain very terrible great sorrow; this is your universal form.
I, exceedingly attached to objects, bewildered by your maya, wander in the end-less pit of 'mine-ness', Supreme Lord.

I, that very one, have come to you as refuge, immeasurable, Lord, worthy of praise, the supreme state, since nothing else; my mind scorched by the weariness and torment of worldly existence, disgusted, longing for the matured abode."
Lakshmi gave him a garland of unfading lotuses sent by Varuna and blue garments fit for the ocean.
Wearing an ear-ornament, adorned with lovely earrings, wearing blue garments and a garland, he then shone with radiance.
Thus adorned, Rama then sported in Vraja; after two months he went again to Mathura city.
Bala married Revati, daughter of King Raivata, and on her were born Nishatha and Ulmuka.
Who is this, how has he come into the fish's belly? Thus Narada said to the slender woman seized with curiosity:

This is Krishna's son, stolen from the lying-in room by Shambara, the maker of creation and dissolution of all worlds.
brahmapuran:200:10	Thrown into the sea, he was swallowed by a fish and has come into your power. This is a jewel among men, fair-browed; protect him with trust.
Thus told by Narada, she nursed that child, deluded from childhood by great love and surpassing beauty.
When he was adorned with youth, best of Brahmins, the elephant-gaited one then became filled with desire.
Mayavati gave all the maya to that great-souled one, Pradyumna, as her own; her heart and eyes fixed on him. To her, clinging, that lotus-eyed son of Krishna said:
